resumen: The bench press with the back rest inclined to about 30°: the bar comes down to the upper chest. It shifts some of the work towards the upper chest and the shoulder.
ejecucion: Set the back rest to about 30° and the safety pins just below where the bar touches your chest, or have someone spot you: getting stuck under the bar is the serious accident in this lift.
Sit with your back against the back rest, shoulder blades squeezed together against it and feet on the floor, and grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders, wrists straight.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your shoulders, arms straight.
Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, below the collarbones, with your elbows at about 45-60° from your torso, not flared out to shoulder height.
Press up until your arms are straight, without lifting your back or glutes off the bench.
When the set is done, bring the bar back to the rack and make sure it is resting before you let go.
matices: In a study of thirty trained people and five inclinations, the upper chest was most active at 30°, and above 45° the anterior deltoid took over. Another, in fifteen men, found the clavicular portion more active at 44° than at 28° or flat, and the sternal portion more active flat. They disagree on the exact angle; what they share is that inclining favours the upper chest and the shoulder at the expense of the lower chest. A third study, with eight people and high-density electrodes, saw the centre of pectoral activity shift towards the clavicular portion at 45°. The authors of the second recommend doing both flat and incline pressing.
